images.caption: Figure 1:COSMI.Left: sequences of the COSMI dataset, composed from single-object captures and rendered with clothed scans. Right: composition of one sequence from a sitting clip, a right-hand action, a left-hand action obtained by mirroring, and a backpack, rendered with a clothed scan.

Figure 2:Composition of one sequence.Atomic clips are extracted by interaction rules, annotated by a language model, and mirrored. A sitting target receives two compatible hand actions, their limbs and objects are transferred onto its body, and the caption is assembled accordingly.

Figure 3:COSMI method.One transformer denoises thehuman tokensℋ\mathcal{H}, one per frame, and theobject tokens𝒪n\mathcal{O}_{n}, one per four frames, atdiffusion steptt. Conditioned on the CLIPtext tokens𝒲\mathcal{W}, theinitial poses, and thenameandBPSgeometry of every object, it generates the human motion and each object motion relative to the joint that drives it.

Figure 4:Hand-object recordings as source clips.A HOT3D recording of the hands and the object (left) becomes a full-body clip once SMPL-X is fitted to the headset and the MANO hands (middle), and the composition pairs it with a sitting clip like any captured source (right).
Figure 5:Qualitative comparison.Generations for a test prompt with the unseen black chair and two hand actions in sequence. COSMI keeps the person seated, and generates plausible contacts.

Figure 6:Qualitative comparison with the baselines.Generations for test prompts of the three-object tier (top) and of the all-objects tier (bottom), which includes more than 3 objects and therefore no HIMO. COSMI keeps every object in the hand that drives it, whereas the baselines let objects drift away from the hands or float beside the body.
Figure 7:Failure cases.Left: the hinge of the flip phone has limited movement range. Right: the unseen black chair is placed off the body, which intersects its armrest.

Figure 8:Hand-object recordings as source clips.A HOT3D recording (second column) provides the hands and the object. A body fitted to the head-mounted device and the MANO hands (third column) turns it into a source clip, which the rules and the composition process like any other, here onto sitting and large-object targets (first column), giving the composed sequences (fourth column).

Figure 9:Clothed scans animated with composed sequences.4D-DRESS scans (left), registered as SMPL-X+D, are driven by the joint transforms of composed sequences, shown on the body model in the top row. Objects follow through their joint-relative transforms, and the finger motion is preserved on the hands.

Figure 10:Atomic clips per interaction rule.Clips extracted by each of the thirteen rules ofTable6, the walking sequences of AMASS included. Target rules (T) engage the whole body, source rules (S) one or both hands, and augmentation rules (A) worn objects. Holds and worn objects are single frames.

Figure 12:Mirroring.Global reflection of the object breaks the contact with the mirrored hand, and local reflection keeps the contact but mirrors the mesh. Our local mirroring poses the original mesh like its reflection with a proper rotation and preserves both.

Figure 14:Composition of sequences.Left: the target clip, which provides the body motion, and the source clips, whose limbs are colored, blue for the left hand, red for the right hand, and purple for both hands. Right: the composed sequence, in which the source limbs replace their counterparts and every object follows its limb throughEq.1. Rows two and four are sequential compositions.
Figure 15:Sequences of the COSMI dataset.Composed sequences with their captions: simultaneous and sequential actions on walking, sitting, and standing bodies, with worn and articulated objects.
